body.value: Londonderry August the 5th 1825 Dear Brother Received your letter of the 30th of May on the 18th of June and agreeable to your request delayed writing until I received your letters of July 6 which came to hand on the 30th July. The delay suited me well well as we had pretty trying times in June, Spring having commenced so early together with an excessive drought that I brought hay-making and harvest in as early and as I earlier, to best of my recollection than we pain of this kind of harvesting on the 23 earlier I began to commence mowing on the 11 of June however you are a competent judge. Our crops was shortness light and short overing to the warmth and yet for besides our calculations. The retro not being boldtown was scarce worth mentioning, the weather for hay making was just the reverse of last year very fine. The grain however made ample and amends for we have the greatest crop of Wheat and Rye taken together that ever was raised on the place. The wheat at age rate is the greatest. We have 993 dozens of Wheat and 561 of Rye. The oats was not good we harvest but 526 lots its Harvest looks clouds was 66cts. the average hay-making and until lately cost 5.62 its harvest lasted just 2 weeks. The drought this season has exceeded any forfeiture known in this country. I was obliged to give flooding in the latter end of May for about 8 days, the weather was so very hot and the ground of such an absorption the Propertie of a dungeon in its, and the pasturage was so completely dried up the stock had to drink from the pump & carried to them in great labour & dearest water – we have had no rain to speak of since 18th April. Agreeably to your request I continue to forward you examms of our slaughter calculations. The price of Beef has declined to 3d to 4d the lb. Mutton 4d to 5d and Pork from 3d to 4d. The price of Lamb is very low. The demand for Potatoes very great and the price 16cts the stone (14lbs) for good sorts. The price for other articles is very variable, Butter 5d to 8d. Eggs 2d to 3d the dozen. The flax crop promises to be very good – I sell to Mr. John Irwin at 30 cts. the stones. He said he had offered 32 cts. to others for those of a superior quality. My family is perfectly well busy preparing for the meeting of my son John who is expected here on the 15th of September from Edinburgh where he has been completing his Studies in Medicine, an application has been made from the inhabitants of this place to my son to settle here as a Physician – I believe he is not disposed to accept the invitation. I remain in perfect harmony with my neighbors & customers. I remain Dear brother your affectionate brother James Mayne
